w: Built from 1309 by the Knights Hospitaller over existing Byzantine walls, these fortifications form a defensive crescent around the medieval town, rubble-cored masonry built to absorb cannon fire. Each stretch was held by a different Langue - France, Spain, Germany, Italy - and bastions still carry their names.
s: Knights' walls, each stretch held by a different tongue
_facts: Built from 1309 by the Knights Hospitaller, enhancing existing Byzantine walls
Rubble masonry construction designed to withstand gunshots
Different sections defended by different Langue (tongues) of Knights: Grand Master, France/Auvergne, Spain, Germany, Italy
Bastions and terrepleins still carry the names of their assigned Langue

w: Also known as the Hydrobiological Station, this research center and aquarium dates to the 1930s, when Rhodes was under Italian rule. It still functions as a working marine research facility as much as a visitor attraction, now run by the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research.
s: A 1930s Italian-era aquarium and research station
_facts: Also known as the Hydrobiological Station of Rhodes
Built in the 1930s under Italian rule
Now administered by the Hellenic Centre for Marine Research

w: Founded in 1793 by Hafiz Ahmed Agha, this Ottoman library still stands inside the walls of Rhodes' medieval city, itself a UNESCO World Heritage Site - a quiet survivor from the last century of Ottoman rule on the island.
s: An Ottoman library inside the walled old town
_facts: Historic Ottoman building in the medieval city of Rhodes, a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Founded by Hafiz Ahmed Agha in 1793

n: Church of St John of the Collachium
w: The Knights Hospitaller's conventual church, built beside the Grand Master's palace in the 1300s, held relics tied to John the Baptist, with six grand masters buried inside. It became the town's main mosque after 1522 - then in 1856 a lightning strike ignited stored gunpowder, killing 200 and leveling it.
s: The Knights' church, blown up by its own gunpowder
_facts: Built by the Knights Hospitaller in the first half of the 14th century, dedicated to John the Baptist
Conventual church adjacent to the Palace of the Grand Master; six grand masters buried there
Became the town's main mosque after the 1522 Ottoman conquest
Destroyed 6 November 1856 by a lightning strike that ignited stored gunpowder, killing at least 200

w: Founded in 1997 by Aron Hasson of the Rhodes Jewish Historical Foundation, this museum occupies six rooms that once served as the women's prayer galleries of the adjoining Kahal Shalom Synagogue - the oldest synagogue in Greece.
s: Jewish history told from the old synagogue's gallery
_facts: Established 1997 by Aron Hasson of the Rhodes Jewish Historical Foundation
Located in the Old Town, adjacent to the Kahal Shalom Synagogue
Housed in six rooms formerly used as the synagogue's women's prayer rooms

w: Dating to the 4th century BC or the start of the Hellenistic era, this modest stone span is the oldest known Greek bridge built with a voussoir arch - the wedge-stone technique that later defined Roman engineering. Easy to walk past without noticing.
s: The oldest known Greek arch bridge
_facts: Ancient Greek arch bridge dating to the 4th century BC or early Hellenistic period
Oldest known Greek bridge built with a voussoir arch

w: Built around 1887, in the final decades of Ottoman rule on Rhodes, this is one of the smaller, plainer mosques inside the walled town - no grand dome, just a modest prayer hall. It has stood abandoned for decades, no longer used for worship.
s: A modest late-Ottoman mosque, long abandoned
_facts: Built c. 1887 during the Ottoman era
One of the smaller, simpler mosques on the island
Abandoned, not used for worship

w: Chares of Lindos raised this 33-metre bronze Helios in 280 BC to mark Rhodes surviving a year-long siege by Demetrius I of Macedon. An earthquake toppled it in 226 BC; the Oracle of Delphi advised against rebuilding, so it lay in pieces until an Arab force broke it up for scrap in 653.
s: The fallen Wonder that gave Rhodes its name
_facts: Statue of Helios by Chares of Lindos, erected 280 BC, one of the Seven Wonders
About 33 metres (108 ft) tall, roughly two-thirds the height of the Statue of Liberty
Collapsed in the earthquake of 226 BC; never rebuilt per the Oracle of Delphi
Remains destroyed/sold after the Arab conquest of 653

n: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes
w: Known locally as the Kastello, this castle served the Knights Hospitaller as palace, headquarters and fortress all at once - one of the few substantial examples of Gothic architecture surviving in Greece, seat of the grand masters' rule over Rhodes.
_facts: Also known as the Kastello, a medieval castle in the city of Rhodes
One of the few examples of Gothic architecture in Greece
Previously a Knights Hospitaller citadel functioning as palace, headquarters, and fortress

w: Built up between 1309 and 1523 under the Knights Hospitaller, this walled quarter splits into a high town in the north and a lower town to the south-southwest, still enclosed by a 4-kilometer wall. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1988.
s: The Knights' walled town, still lived in today
_facts: Constructed c. 1309-1523 under the Knights Hospitaller
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988
Consists of a high town (north) and lower town (south-southwest) within a 4 km wall

w: Completed in 1577 in what was once La Juderia, the Jewish quarter of Rhodes, this is the oldest synagogue in Greece. Its congregation still worships in the Eastern Sephardi rite, mostly in summer, and the building also houses the Jewish Museum of Rhodes.
s: Greece's oldest synagogue, still holding services
_facts: Completed 1577; the oldest synagogue in Greece
Located in La Juderia, the former Jewish quarter of Rhodes
Worships in the Eastern Sephardi rite, mainly in summer; houses the Jewish Museum of Rhodes

w: Sitting on Monte Smith, three kilometers from the modern city, this 5th-century BC upper town held temples to Athena Polias, Zeus Polieus and Apollo, with a stadium, odeon and gymnasium below. Unusually, the ancient Rhodians never walled it as a citadel.
s: The unfortified acropolis on Monte Smith
_facts: Upper town of ancient Rhodes, dating from the 5th century BC, 3 km SW of the modern city on Monte Smith
Includes the Temple of Athena Polias and Zeus Polieus and the Temple of Apollo
Also has a stadium, odeon, and gymnasium
Unlike other acropoleis, was never enclosed as a walled citadel

w: Completed around 1623 and named for Ottoman admiral Murat Reis the Elder, this mosque inside the old walled town was abandoned in the 1940s. Its minaret is a curiosity - a replacement built under Italian administration, not the Ottoman original.
s: A mosque named for an Ottoman admiral, oddly minareted
_facts: Completed c. 1623 during the Ottoman era, named after admiral Murat Reis the Elder
Abandoned in the 1940s
Unusual minaret is a post-Ottoman replacement built under Italian administration

w: Completed around 1541, this is the oldest of the seven mosques still standing inside Rhodes' old walled city, and the only one still open for worship. The others have been abandoned or converted; this one still serves the Turkish-Muslim community.
s: The oldest mosque in the old town, still in use
_facts: Completed c. 1541, the oldest of the seven mosques inside the old walled city
The only one of the seven still open for worship
Serves the Turkish-Muslim community of Rhodes

w: Built in the thirteenth century within the walled city, this Byzantine-era church spent the Ottoman period repurposed as a mosque, Kavakli Mescidi. It returned to Christian worship in the early twentieth century - Byzantine, then Ottoman, then Orthodox again.
s: A Byzantine church that spent centuries as a mosque
_facts: Greek Orthodox church built in the 13th century within the old walled city
Converted into a mosque (Kavakli Mescidi) during the Ottoman era
Returned to Christian worship in the early 20th century
